Receding-Horizon Control

An open-loop trajectory specifies controls from an initial state to a final time. During execution, the control ut\mathbf u_tut​ depends only on the clock, reading precomputed values or interpolating between them. The MPPI examples already used a different execution rule: apply one action, observe the new state, and update the remaining plan. Receding-horizon control applies this rule to any suitable finite-horizon optimizer, including the transcription methods developed in the preceding chapters.

Real systems face modeling errors, external disturbances, and measurement noise that accumulate over time. A precomputed trajectory becomes increasingly irrelevant as these perturbations push the actual system state away from the predicted path. The solution is to incorporate feedback, making control decisions that respond to the current state rather than blindly following a predetermined schedule. While dynamic programming provides the theoretical framework for deriving feedback policies through value functions and Bellman equations, there exists a more direct approach that leverages the trajectory optimization methods already developed.

Can the finite-horizon planner itself become a feedback controller by solving again whenever a new state is measured?

Learning Goals¶

After working through the derivations and the balancing example, you should be able to:

  • Turn a finite-horizon optimal-control problem into a state-feedback law by replanning, and state the feedback law and its domain precisely.

  • Explain why a short horizon without terminal ingredients can leave an unstable system uncontrolled, stall it near a constraint, or lose feasibility.

  • Prove recursive feasibility and closed-loop convergence from a terminal cost, a terminal set, and a local controller, using the shifted candidate sequence.

  • Construct a quadratic terminal cost and an ellipsoidal terminal set for a linear system with box constraints, and check both numerically.

  • Decide when the finite-horizon value is a lower bound, an upper bound, or neither, for the infinite-horizon value.

Prerequisites¶

The chapter uses the finite-horizon optimal-control formulation, the transcription methods that turn it into a nonlinear program, and the receding-horizon execution used by MPPI. The worked example solves small convex quadratic programs; only the facts that such programs have a unique solution and can be solved reliably are needed. Dynamic programming and the linear-quadratic regulator are not required. Where the example uses an LQR gain, the property it relies on is derived here.

Closing the Loop by Replanning¶

Which action from each finite-horizon solution should be applied before the state is measured and the horizon is shifted forward?

Model Predictive Control creates a feedback controller by repeatedly solving trajectory optimization problems. Rather than computing a single trajectory for the entire task duration, MPC solves a finite-horizon problem at each time step, starting from the current measured state. The controller then applies only the first control action from this solution before repeating the entire process. This strategy transforms any trajectory optimization method into a feedback controller.

The battery example in Model Interfaces used a transparent current governor: it tested a local voltage and thermal envelope after updating one resistance parameter. MPC retains that structured model but optimizes an entire future current sequence and repeats the optimization as measurements arrive.

The Receding Horizon Principle¶

The defining characteristic of MPC is its receding horizon strategy. At each time step, the controller solves an optimization problem looking a fixed duration into the future, but this prediction window constantly moves forward in time. The horizon “recedes” because it always starts from the current time and extends forward by the same amount.

Consider the discrete-time optimal control problem in Bolza form:

minimizecN(xN)+∑k=0N−1ck(xk,uk)subject toxk+1=fk(xk,uk)gk(xk,uk)≤0xmin≤xk≤xmaxumin≤uk≤umaxgivenx0=xcurrent\begin{aligned} \text{minimize} \quad & c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\ \text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\ & \mathbf{g}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \leq \mathbf{0} \\ & \mathbf{x}_{\text{min}} \leq \mathbf{x}_k \leq \mathbf{x}_{\text{max}} \\ & \mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \leq \mathbf{u}_k \leq \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}} \\ \text{given} \quad & \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{current}} \end{aligned}minimizesubject togiven​cN​(xN​)+k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​,uk​)xk+1​=fk​(xk​,uk​)gk​(xk​,uk​)≤0xmin​≤xk​≤xmax​umin​≤uk​≤umax​x0​=xcurrent​​
(1)

This is the Bolza problem of Finite-Horizon Optimal Control Problems, with its index counted from the current time rather than from the start of the task. If the state is measured at time ttt, then x0=xcurrent\mathbf x_0=\mathbf x_{\text{current}}x0​=xcurrent​ is that measurement, xk\mathbf x_kxk​ is the state predicted for time t+kt+kt+k, and the NNN controls u0,…,uN−1\mathbf u_0,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}u0​,…,uN−1​ span the prediction horizon, as in the MPPI algorithm. For a time-varying task, ckc_kck​, fk\mathbf f_kfk​, and gk\mathbf g_kgk​ are the stage cost, dynamics, and constraints of time t+kt+kt+k. The terminal cost cNc_NcN​ is charged at the end of the prediction horizon, not at the end of the task.

At time step ttt, this problem optimizes over the interval [t,t+N][t, t+N][t,t+N]. At the next time step t+1t+1t+1, the horizon shifts to [t+1,t+N+1][t+1, t+N+1][t+1,t+N+1]. What makes this work is that only the first control u0⋆\mathbf{u}_0^\staru0⋆​ from each optimization is applied. The remaining controls u1⋆,…,uN−1⋆\mathbf{u}_1^\star, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_{N-1}^\staru1⋆​,…,uN−1⋆​ are discarded, though they may initialize the next optimization through warm-starting.

This receding horizon principle enables feedback without computing an explicit policy. By constantly updating predictions based on current measurements, MPC naturally corrects for disturbances and model errors. The apparent waste of computing but not using most of the trajectory is actually the mechanism that provides robustness.

A Balancing Example¶

Balancing a stick upright on a fingertip shows what replanning buys. The upright position is an equilibrium, but a small tilt grows on its own, so a precomputed command sequence that is slightly wrong does not stay slightly wrong. Linearized about the upright position, the angle θ\thetaθ obeys

θ¨=gℓ θ+u,\ddot\theta = \frac{g}{\ell}\,\theta + u ,θ¨=ℓg​θ+u,
(2)

where ℓ\ellℓ is the stick length and uuu is the angular acceleration commanded through the fingertip. With g=9.81g=9.81g=9.81 m/s2^22 and ℓ=1\ell=1ℓ=1 m, a tilt grows by a factor eee about every ℓ/g≈0.32\sqrt{\ell/g}\approx 0.32ℓ/g​≈0.32 s. We sample the model exactly under a zero-order hold with period Δt=0.05\Delta t=0.05Δt=0.05 s, which gives a linear model xk+1=Axk+Buk\mathbf x_{k+1}=A\mathbf x_k+B u_kxk+1​=Axk​+Buk​ with x=(θ,θ˙)\mathbf x=(\theta,\dot\theta)x=(θ,θ˙). The command is limited to ∣uk∣≤5|u_k|\le 5∣uk​∣≤5 rad/s2^22, and the angle must stay within ∣θk∣≤0.35|\theta_k|\le 0.35∣θk​∣≤0.35 rad. The stage cost is quadratic,

c(x,u)=x⊤Qx+Ru2,Q=diag⁡(10,1),R=0.05.c(\mathbf x,u)=\mathbf x^\top Q\mathbf x+R u^2,\qquad Q=\operatorname{diag}(10,1),\quad R=0.05 .c(x,u)=x⊤Qx+Ru2,Q=diag(10,1),R=0.05.
(3)

Each MPC subproblem is therefore a convex quadratic program in the NNN commands and N+1N+1N+1 predicted states. The terminal cost x⊤Px\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xx⊤Px and the terminal set {x:x⊤Px≤α}\{\mathbf x:\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha\}{x:x⊤Px≤α} used in this section are constructed in Constructing Terminal Ingredients. For now, treat them as given.

The experiment starts from x0=(0.2, 0.6)\mathbf x_0=(0.2,\,0.6)x0​=(0.2,0.6): tilted and falling further. A plan with horizon N=40N=40N=40 (two seconds) is computed once from the nominal model. Two executions of that plan are then compared on a plant whose stick is 15% shorter than the model assumes, and which receives a tap on its angular rate of 0.5 rad/s at t=1t=1t=1 s. The first execution applies the 40 planned commands open loop. The second solves the same problem again from every measured state and applies only the first command.

Before looking at the result, predict which effect hurts the open-loop execution first: the shorter stick or the tap.

The model error alone defeats the open-loop plan. The shorter stick falls faster than predicted, the planned commands are too small to catch it, and the angle leaves its limit at t=0.85t=0.85t=0.85 s, before the tap arrives. The open-loop execution never measures the state, so it cannot detect the error. The replanned controller solves the same optimization with the same wrong model, but each new solve starts from the measured state, so the accumulated prediction error is corrected one step at a time. Every one of its 60 subproblems is feasible, and the tap appears only as a second burst of command. Replanning does not repair the model. It limits how long a model error can act before it is measured.

The Controller Defined by Replanning¶

For a time-invariant problem, such as regulation of the stick, the subproblem depends on the time ttt only through its initial state. Write u0⋆(x)\mathbf u_0^\star(\mathbf x)u0⋆​(x) for the first optimal command when the subproblem starts from x\mathbf xx. Replanning then executes the state-feedback law

κN(x)=u0⋆(x),xt+1=f(xt,κN(xt)).\kappa_N(\mathbf x)=\mathbf u_0^\star(\mathbf x),\qquad \mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf f\big(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t)\big).κN​(x)=u0⋆​(x),xt+1​=f(xt​,κN​(xt​)).
(4)

The law is defined only where the subproblem has a solution. Call this set the feasible set XN\mathcal X_NXN​: the states from which some admissible command sequence of length NNN satisfies every constraint and ends in the terminal set. The law κN\kappa_NκN​ is never written down. It is evaluated one state at a time by an optimizer. The parametric controllers chapter studies the map x↦κN(x)\mathbf x\mapsto\kappa_N(\mathbf x)x↦κN​(x) as an object in its own right. For linear dynamics, quadratic costs, and polyhedral constraints, it is a continuous piecewise affine function of the state Bemporad et al. (2002).

Figure 2 shows both objects for the stick. The feasible sets are nested, X5⊂X10⊂X20\mathcal X_5\subset\mathcal X_{10}\subset\mathcal X_{20}X5​⊂X10​⊂X20​: a longer horizon allows more steps to reach the terminal ellipse, so more initial states qualify. On the grid they cover 35%, 43%, and 49% of the plotted rectangle. The initial state (0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6) lies outside the terminal ellipse, and nine steps are the fewest that reach it. Outside the shaded bands the stick is falling too fast in the direction of its tilt to be caught by commands of at most 5 rad/s2^22 without violating the angle limit.

The right panel contains a lesson specific to this small example. Wherever the subproblem is feasible, κ20\kappa_{20}κ20​ agrees with the saturated linear law sat⁡(Kx)\operatorname{sat}(K\mathbf x)sat(Kx) to within 4×10−54\times10^{-5}4×10−5 rad/s2^22, where KKK is the LQR gain from which the terminal cost is built. For a two-dimensional state with one input, the active constraint along optimal paths is usually the input bound at the first step, and the optimizer rediscovers saturation. The optimizer adds two things that the saturated law lacks. First, it reports a state outside X20\mathcal X_{20}X20​ as infeasible instead of returning a command that cannot succeed. Second, the stability argument below comes with it. With more states, more inputs, or state constraints that become active along the way, the optimizer’s law departs from any saturated linear law.

Warm starting fits naturally here. Consecutive states are close, so the shifted previous solution (u1⋆,…,uN−1⋆,uN−1⋆)(\mathbf u_1^\star,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star)(u1⋆​,…,uN−1⋆​,uN−1⋆​) is a good initial guess for the next solve. The proof of stability below uses almost the same shifted sequence, with the last entry chosen more carefully.

Horizon Selection and Problem Formulation¶

The choice of prediction horizon depends on the control objective. We distinguish between three cases, each requiring different mathematical formulations.

Infinite-Horizon Regulation¶

For stabilization problems where the system must operate indefinitely around an equilibrium, the dynamics, constraints, and stage cost are usually time-invariant, so we drop their index: fk=f\mathbf f_k=\mathbf ffk​=f, gk=g\mathbf g_k=\mathbf ggk​=g, and ck=cc_k=cck​=c. The true objective is:

J∞=∑k=0∞c(xk,uk)J_\infty = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k)J∞​=k=0∑∞​c(xk​,uk​)
(5)

Since this cannot be solved directly, MPC approximates it with:

minimizecN(xN)+∑k=0N−1c(xk,uk)subject toxk+1=f(xk,uk)xN∈Xfother constraints\begin{aligned} \text{minimize} \quad & c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\ \text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\ & \mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f \\ & \text{other constraints} \end{aligned}minimizesubject to​cN​(xN​)+k=0∑N−1​c(xk​,uk​)xk+1​=f(xk​,uk​)xN​∈Xf​other constraints​
(6)

The terminal cost cN(xN)c_N(\mathbf{x}_N)cN​(xN​) approximates ∑k=N∞c(xk,uk)\sum_{k=N}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k)∑k=N∞​c(xk​,uk​), the cost-to-go beyond the horizon. The terminal constraint xN∈Xf\mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_fxN​∈Xf​ ensures the state reaches a region where a known stabilizing controller exists. Without these terminal ingredients, the finite-horizon approximation may produce unstable behavior, as the controller ignores consequences beyond the horizon.

Finite-Duration Tasks¶

For a task ending at time TTT, the true objective from the current time ttt is the remaining part of the Bolza objective, written in absolute time:

J[t,T]=cT(xT)+∑s=tT−1cs(xs,us)J_{[t, T]} = c_T(\mathbf{x}_T) + \sum_{s=t}^{T-1} c_s(\mathbf{x}_s, \mathbf{u}_s)J[t,T]​=cT​(xT​)+s=t∑T−1​cs​(xs​,us​)
(7)

The MPC formulation must adapt as time progresses. While the end of the task lies beyond the prediction horizon, the subproblem keeps the surrogate terminal cost cNc_NcN​. Once t+N≥Tt+N\geq Tt+N≥T, the horizon shrinks to the T−tT-tT−t remaining steps:

minimize{cN(xN)+∑k=0N−1ck(xk,uk),t+N<T,cT(xT−t)+∑k=0T−t−1ck(xk,uk),t+N≥T.\text{minimize} \quad \begin{cases} c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) + \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k), & t+N < T, \\[2ex] c_T(\mathbf{x}_{T-t}) + \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k), & t+N \geq T. \end{cases}minimize⎩⎨⎧​cN​(xN​)+k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​,uk​),cT​(xT−t​)+k=0∑T−t−1​ck​(xk​,uk​),​t+N<T,t+N≥T.​
(8)

In the second case, xT−t\mathbf{x}_{T-t}xT−t​ is the prediction of the final state xT\mathbf{x}_TxT​, so the task’s own terminal cost applies. As the task approaches completion, the horizon shrinks and the terminal cost switches from the approximation cNc_NcN​ to the true final cost cTc_TcT​. This prevents the controller from optimizing beyond task completion, which would produce meaningless or aggressive control actions.

Periodic Tasks¶

Some systems operate on repeating cycles where the optimal behavior depends on the time of day, week, or season. Consider a commercial building where heating costs are higher at night, electricity prices vary hourly, and occupancy patterns repeat daily. The MPC controller must account for these periodic patterns while planning over a finite horizon.

For tasks with period TpT_pTp​, such as daily building operations, the formulation accounts for transitions across period boundaries:

minimize∑k=0N−1ck(xk,uk)whereφk=(t+k)mod  Tpck={cdayif φk∈[6am,6pm]cnightotherwise\begin{aligned} \text{minimize} \quad & \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\ \text{where} \quad & \varphi_k = (t + k) \mod T_p \\ & c_k = \begin{cases} c_{\text{day}} & \text{if } \varphi_k \in [6\text{am}, 6\text{pm}] \\ c_{\text{night}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}minimizewhere​k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​,uk​)φk​=(t+k)modTp​ck​={cday​cnight​​if φk​∈[6am,6pm]otherwise​​
(9)

The stage cost ckc_kck​ changes with the phase φk\varphi_kφk​ of the predicted time t+kt+kt+k within the period. Constraints may similarly depend on the phase, reflecting different operational requirements at different times.

The MPC Algorithm¶

The complete MPC procedure implements the receding horizon principle through repeated optimization:

Algorithm 1 (Model Predictive Control with Horizon Management)

Input:

  • Nominal prediction horizon NNN

  • Sampling period Δt\Delta tΔt

  • Task type: {infinite, finite ending at time TTT, periodic with period TpT_pTp​}

  • Cost functions and dynamics

  • Constraints

Procedure:

  1. Initialize time t←0t \leftarrow 0t←0

  2. Measure initial state xcurrent\mathbf{x}_{\text{current}}xcurrent​

  3. While task continues:

    1. Determine effective horizon and costs:

      • If infinite task:

        • Nt←NN_t \leftarrow NNt​←N

        • Use terminal cost cNc_NcN​ and constraint Xf\mathcal{X}_fXf​

      • If finite task:

        • Nt←min⁡(N,T−t)N_t \leftarrow \min(N, T - t)Nt​←min(N,T−t)

        • If t+Nt=Tt + N_t = Tt+Nt​=T: use final cost cTc_TcT​

        • Otherwise: use approximation cNc_NcN​

      • If periodic task:

        • Nt←NN_t \leftarrow NNt​←N

        • Adjust costs/constraints based on phase

    2. Solve optimization: Minimize over u0:Nt−1\mathbf{u}_{0:N_t-1}u0:Nt​−1​ subject to dynamics, constraints, and x0=xcurrent\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{current}}x0​=xcurrent​

    3. Apply receding horizon control:

      • Extract u0⋆\mathbf{u}^\star_0u0⋆​ from solution

      • Apply to system for duration Δt\Delta tΔt

      • Measure new state xcurrent\mathbf{x}_{\text{current}}xcurrent​

      • Advance time: t←t+1t \leftarrow t + 1t←t+1

  4. End While

Successive Linearization and Quadratic Approximations¶

Any solver that improves one finite-horizon plan by successive approximation can be used inside MPC: solve from the newly observed state, execute the first action, and repeat. The iLQR and DDP chapter, after dynamic programming, develops one such solver. Its backward-pass feedback gains and the outer decision to replan are distinct operations.

For many regulation and tracking problems, the nonlinear dynamics and costs we encounter can be approximated locally by linear and quadratic functions. The basic idea is to linearize the system around the current operating point and approximate the cost with a quadratic form. This reduces each MPC subproblem to a quadratic program (QP), which can be solved reliably and very quickly using standard solvers.

Suppose the true dynamics are nonlinear,

xk+1=fk(xk,uk).\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathbf{u}_k).xk+1​=fk​(xk​,uk​).
(10)

Around a nominal trajectory (xˉk,uˉk)(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k)(xˉk​,uˉk​), we take a first-order expansion:

xk+1≈fk(xˉk,uˉk)+Ak(xk−xˉk)+Bk(uk−uˉk),\mathbf{x}_{k+1} \approx \mathbf{f}_k(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k) + A_k(\mathbf{x}_k - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_k) + B_k(\mathbf{u}_k - \bar{\mathbf{u}}_k),xk+1​≈fk​(xˉk​,uˉk​)+Ak​(xk​−xˉk​)+Bk​(uk​−uˉk​),
(11)

with Jacobians

Ak=∂fk∂x∣(xˉk,uˉk),Bk=∂fk∂u∣(xˉk,uˉk).A_k = \left.\frac{\partial \mathbf{f}_k}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\right|_{(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k)}, \qquad B_k = \left.\frac{\partial \mathbf{f}_k}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\right|_{(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k)}.Ak​=∂x∂fk​​∣∣​(xˉk​,uˉk​)​,Bk​=∂u∂fk​​∣∣​(xˉk​,uˉk​)​.
(12)

Similarly, if the stage cost is nonlinear,

ck(xk,uk),c_k(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathbf{u}_k),ck​(xk​,uk​),
(13)

we approximate it quadratically near the nominal point:

ck(xk,uk)  ≈  ∥xk−xkref∥Qk2+∥uk−ukref∥Rk2,c_k(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathbf{u}_k) \;\approx\; \|\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{Q_k}^2 + \|\mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{u}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{R_k}^2,ck​(xk​,uk​)≈∥xk​−xkref​∥Qk​2​+∥uk​−ukref​∥Rk​2​,
(14)

with positive semidefinite weighting matrices QkQ_kQk​ and RkR_kRk​, where ∥v∥Q2=v⊤Q v\|\mathbf{v}\|_{Q}^2=\mathbf{v}^\top Q\,\mathbf{v}∥v∥Q2​=v⊤Qv.

The resulting MPC subproblem has the form

min⁡x0:N,u0:N−1∥xN−xNref∥P2+∑k=0N−1(∥xk−xkref∥Qk2+∥uk−ukref∥Rk2)s.t.xk+1=Akxk+Bkuk+dk,umin⁡≤uk≤umax⁡,xmin⁡≤xk≤xmax⁡,x0=xcurrent,\begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{x}_{0:N},\mathbf{u}_{0:N-1}} \quad & \|\mathbf{x}_N - \mathbf{x}_N^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{P}^2 + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( \|\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{Q_k}^2 + \|\mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{u}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{R_k}^2 \right) \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A_k \mathbf{x}_k + B_k \mathbf{u}_k + \mathbf{d}_k, \\ & \mathbf{u}_{\min} \leq \mathbf{u}_k \leq \mathbf{u}_{\max}, \\ & \mathbf{x}_{\min} \leq \mathbf{x}_k \leq \mathbf{x}_{\max}, \\ & \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{current}} , \end{aligned}x0:N​,u0:N−1​min​s.t.​∥xN​−xNref​∥P2​+k=0∑N−1​(∥xk​−xkref​∥Qk​2​+∥uk​−ukref​∥Rk​2​)xk+1​=Ak​xk​+Bk​uk​+dk​,umin​≤uk​≤umax​,xmin​≤xk​≤xmax​,x0​=xcurrent​,​
(15)

where dk=fk(xˉk,uˉk)−Akxˉk−Bkuˉk\mathbf{d}_k = \mathbf{f}_k(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_k) - A_k \bar{\mathbf{x}}_k - B_k \bar{\mathbf{u}}_kdk​=fk​(xˉk​,uˉk​)−Ak​xˉk​−Bk​uˉk​ captures the local affine offset. The terminal weight PPP plays the role of the terminal cost cNc_NcN​.

Because the dynamics are now linear and the cost quadratic, this optimization problem is a convex quadratic program. Quadratic programs are attractive in practice: they can be solved at kilohertz rates with mature numerical methods, making them the backbone of many real-time MPC implementations.

At each MPC step, the controller updates its linearization around the new operating point, constructs the local QP, and solves it. The process repeats, with the linear model and quadratic cost refreshed at every reoptimization. Despite the approximation, this yields a closed-loop controller that inherits the fast computation of QPs while retaining the ability to track trajectories of the underlying nonlinear system.

Theoretical Guarantees¶

Repeated optimization creates feedback, but which terminal ingredients make feasibility persist and the closed-loop state converge?

The finite-horizon approximation in MPC brings a new challenge: the controller cannot see consequences beyond the horizon. Without proper design, this myopia can destabilize even simple systems. The solution is to carefully encode information about the infinite-horizon problem into the finite-horizon optimization through its terminal conditions.

Before diving into the mathematics, we should first establish what “stability” means and which tasks these theoretical guarantees address, as the notion of stability varies significantly across different control objectives.

Stability Notions Across Control Tasks¶

The terminal conditions provide different types of guarantees depending on the control objective. For regulation problems, where the task is to drive the state to a fixed equilibrium (xeq,ueq)(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{eq}, \mathbf{u}_\mathrm{eq})(xeq​,ueq​) (often shifted to the origin), the stability guarantee is asymptotic stability: starting sufficiently close to the equilibrium, the closed-loop state satisfies xt→xeq\mathbf{x}_t \to \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{eq}xt​→xeq​ as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞ while constraints remain satisfied throughout the trajectory (recursive feasibility). This requires the stage cost c(x,u)c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u})c(x,u) to be positive definite in the deviation from equilibrium.

When tracking a constant setpoint, the task becomes following a constant reference (xref,uref)(\mathbf{x}^\mathrm{ref},\mathbf{u}^\mathrm{ref})(xref,uref) that solves the steady-state equations. This problem is handled by working in error coordinates x~=x−xref\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^\mathrm{ref}x~=x−xref and u~=u−uref\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^\mathrm{ref}u~=u−uref, transforming the tracking problem into a regulation problem for the error system. The stability guarantee becomes asymptotic tracking, meaning x~t→0\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_t \to \mathbf{0}x~t​→0, again with recursive feasibility.

The terminal conditions we discuss below primarily address regulation and constant reference tracking. Time-varying tracking and economic MPC require additional techniques such as tube MPC and dissipativity theory.

What Goes Wrong Without Terminal Ingredients¶

Remove the terminal cost and the terminal set from the stick controller and keep everything else. Figure 3 shows the closed loop from the same initial state for several horizons, on the exact model and without disturbances.

The failures differ in kind, and each one has a clear cause.

  • With N=1N=1N=1, the objective is c(x0,u0)c(\mathbf x_0,u_0)c(x0​,u0​), and the next state does not enter it. Since x0\mathbf x_0x0​ is fixed, the minimizer is the cheapest command, u0=0u_0=0u0​=0, unless a constraint on x1\mathbf x_1x1​ forces more. The controller does nothing until the angle limit is about to be crossed, and by then no admissible command can prevent it: the subproblem at step 3 is infeasible.

  • With N=3N=3N=3, the horizon covers 0.15 s, less than half the time the tilt needs to grow by a factor eee. Within that window, pushing the stick back costs command effort and returns little angle cost, so the plan does only what is needed to keep the predicted angle under its limit. The subproblem again becomes infeasible at step 3.

  • With N=5N=5N=5, every subproblem is feasible, but the closed loop converges to θ≈0.32\theta\approx0.32θ≈0.32 rad, not to the upright position. There, each plan holds the stick with a constant command and keeps the predicted angle just inside the limit at the end of the horizon. The replanning law has acquired a second equilibrium. Convergence to the target is therefore not implied by feasibility.

  • With N=10N=10N=10, the horizon is long enough, and the stick returns upright. Its closed-loop cost is 20.83, against 20.15 with terminal ingredients. The remaining gap is the price of a horizon that sees only part of the recovery.

A long enough horizon eventually stabilizes the system without any terminal ingredients, and there is a theory that quantifies “long enough” Grüne & Pannek (2017). The required length depends on the system and the initial state, and nothing in the subproblem reports when it is too short. The terminal ingredients make a different trade. They give a certificate that holds for every horizon, at the cost of a smaller feasible set: with the terminal set, the same initial state is infeasible for every N≤8N\le 8N≤8.

MPC with Stability Guarantees¶

To provide theoretical guarantees, the finite-horizon MPC problem is augmented with three interconnected components. The terminal cost cN(x)c_N(\mathbf{x})cN​(x) approximates the cost-to-go beyond the horizon, providing a surrogate for the infinite-horizon tail that cannot be explicitly optimized. The terminal constraint set Xf\mathcal{X}_fXf​ defines a region where we have local knowledge of how to stabilize the system. Finally, the terminal controller πf(x)\pi_f(\mathbf{x})πf​(x) is a local feedback policy that stabilizes the system within Xf\mathcal{X}_fXf​.

These components must satisfy specific compatibility conditions to provide theoretical guarantees. The statement below is for regulation to the origin with time-invariant dynamics f\mathbf ff, stage cost ccc, and constraints g(x,u)≤0\mathbf g(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\le\mathbf 0g(x,u)≤0, which include the state and input bounds. It follows Mayne et al. (2000).

Theorem 1 (Recursive Feasibility and Asymptotic Stability)

Assume that f(0,0)=0\mathbf f(\mathbf 0,\mathbf 0)=\mathbf 0f(0,0)=0, that the stage cost satisfies c(x,u)≥γ∥x∥2c(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\ge\gamma\|\mathbf x\|^2c(x,u)≥γ∥x∥2 for some γ>0\gamma>0γ>0, and that cN≥0c_N\ge 0cN​≥0. Let the terminal set Xf\mathcal X_fXf​ contain the origin, and let the local controller πf\pi_fπf​ satisfy two conditions.

Control invariance: For all x∈Xf\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_fx∈Xf​, we have f(x,πf(x))∈Xf\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x})) \in \mathcal{X}_ff(x,πf​(x))∈Xf​ (the set is invariant) and g(x,πf(x))≤0\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x})) \leq \mathbf{0}g(x,πf​(x))≤0 (constraints remain satisfied).

Lyapunov decrease: For all x∈Xf\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_fx∈Xf​:

cN(f(x,πf(x)))−cN(x)≤−c(x,πf(x))c_N(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x}))) - c_N(\mathbf{x}) \leq -c(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x}))cN​(f(x,πf​(x)))−cN​(x)≤−c(x,πf​(x))
(16)

where ccc is the stage cost.

Suppose that the plant follows the prediction model exactly. Then, for every initial state x0∈XN\mathbf x_0\in\mathcal X_Nx0​∈XN​, the closed loop xt+1=f(xt,κN(xt))\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf f(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))xt+1​=f(xt​,κN​(xt​)) has the following properties:

  1. Recursive feasibility: xt∈XN\mathbf x_t\in\mathcal X_Nxt​∈XN​ for all ttt, so every subproblem has a solution.

  2. Value decrease: VN(xt+1)≤VN(xt)−c(xt,κN(xt))V_N(\mathbf x_{t+1})\le V_N(\mathbf x_t)-c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))VN​(xt+1​)≤VN​(xt​)−c(xt​,κN​(xt​)).

  3. Cost bound and convergence: ∑t=0∞c(xt,κN(xt))≤VN(x0)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0)∑t=0∞​c(xt​,κN​(xt​))≤VN​(x0​), and xt→0\mathbf x_t\to\mathbf 0xt​→0.

Asymptotic stability, in the sense of a Lyapunov function, also needs VNV_NVN​ to be bounded above by a multiple of ∥x∥2\|\mathbf x\|^2∥x∥2 near the origin. This holds, for example, when cNc_NcN​ is quadratic and the origin lies in the interior of Xf\mathcal X_fXf​ Rawlings et al. (2017). The three properties listed are the ones a practitioner relies on, and they follow from one construction.

Proof 1

Fix x∈XN\mathbf x\in\mathcal X_Nx∈XN​ and let (u0⋆,…,uN−1⋆)(\mathbf u_0^\star,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star)(u0⋆​,…,uN−1⋆​) be an optimal solution of the subproblem from x\mathbf xx, with predicted states x0⋆=x,x1⋆,…,xN⋆\mathbf x_0^\star=\mathbf x,\mathbf x_1^\star,\ldots,\mathbf x_N^\starx0⋆​=x,x1⋆​,…,xN⋆​ and xN⋆∈Xf\mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_fxN⋆​∈Xf​. The controller applies u0⋆\mathbf u_0^\staru0⋆​, and since the model is exact, the next state is x+=x1⋆\mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\starx+=x1⋆​.

A feasible candidate from x+\mathbf x^+x+. Consider the shifted sequence

u~=(u1⋆,…,uN−1⋆, πf(xN⋆)).\tilde{\mathbf u}=\big(\mathbf u_1^\star,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star,\ \pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star)\big).u~=(u1⋆​,…,uN−1⋆​, πf​(xN⋆​)).
(17)

From x+\mathbf x^+x+, its first N−1N-1N−1 commands reproduce the predicted states x2⋆,…,xN⋆\mathbf x_2^\star,\ldots,\mathbf x_N^\starx2⋆​,…,xN⋆​, and these satisfy the constraints because they did in the original solution. The last command satisfies g(xN⋆,πf(xN⋆))≤0\mathbf g(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))\le\mathbf 0g(xN⋆​,πf​(xN⋆​))≤0, and the new terminal state f(xN⋆,πf(xN⋆))\mathbf f(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))f(xN⋆​,πf​(xN⋆​)) lies in Xf\mathcal X_fXf​, both by control invariance. Hence u~\tilde{\mathbf u}u~ is feasible, so x+∈XN\mathbf x^+\in\mathcal X_Nx+∈XN​. Induction on ttt proves property 1.

Its cost. The candidate drops the first stage of the original solution and adds one stage under πf\pi_fπf​ at the end. Its cost is

V~=VN(x)−c(x,u0⋆)+[c(xN⋆,πf(xN⋆))+cN(f(xN⋆,πf(xN⋆)))−cN(xN⋆)].\tilde V=V_N(\mathbf x)-c(\mathbf x,\mathbf u_0^\star) +\Big[c(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star)) +c_N\big(\mathbf f(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))\big) -c_N(\mathbf x_N^\star)\Big].V~=VN​(x)−c(x,u0⋆​)+[c(xN⋆​,πf​(xN⋆​))+cN​(f(xN⋆​,πf​(xN⋆​)))−cN​(xN⋆​)].
(18)

The bracket is non-positive by the Lyapunov decrease condition. Since VN(x+)V_N(\mathbf x^+)VN​(x+) is the optimal cost from x+\mathbf x^+x+, it does not exceed the cost of any feasible candidate:

VN(x+)≤V~≤VN(x)−c(x,κN(x)).V_N(\mathbf x^+)\le\tilde V\le V_N(\mathbf x)-c(\mathbf x,\kappa_N(\mathbf x)).VN​(x+)≤V~≤VN​(x)−c(x,κN​(x)).
(19)

This is property 2.

Summing. Adding property 2 over t=0,…,T−1t=0,\ldots,T-1t=0,…,T−1 telescopes to

∑t=0T−1c(xt,κN(xt))≤VN(x0)−VN(xT)≤VN(x0),\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0)-V_N(\mathbf x_T)\le V_N(\mathbf x_0),t=0∑T−1​c(xt​,κN​(xt​))≤VN​(x0​)−VN​(xT​)≤VN​(x0​),
(20)

using VN≥0V_N\ge0VN​≥0. Letting T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞ gives the cost bound. A convergent series of non-negative terms has terms tending to zero, so γ∥xt∥2≤c(xt,κN(xt))→0\gamma\|\mathbf x_t\|^2\le c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\to0γ∥xt​∥2≤c(xt​,κN​(xt​))→0.

The proof never uses optimality of the plan beyond the first step. It compares the new optimum with one feasible candidate. Two practical consequences follow. First, the guarantees survive an inexact solver as long as each returned plan is feasible and costs no more than the shifted candidate. Many real-time implementations check this explicitly and apply the candidate when the solver fails to improve on it. Second, the exact-model assumption enters at exactly one place, x+=x1⋆\mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\starx+=x1⋆​. With model error or disturbances, the measured state differs from the predicted one, and the candidate need not be feasible from it. In Figure 1, the recorded values VN(xt)V_N(\mathbf x_t)VN​(xt​) decrease at every step until the tap, then jump from 0.61 to 3.23. Restoring guarantees under such errors is the subject of robust MPC in the next chapter.

The bound in property 3 also gives a quantitative statement that the stick experiment can check. With terminal ingredients and N=10N=10N=10, the closed-loop cost from x0=(0.2,0.6)\mathbf x_0=(0.2,0.6)x0​=(0.2,0.6) is 20.15, equal to V10(x0)V_{10}(\mathbf x_0)V10​(x0​) to solver precision. The next two subsections explain why the bound is tight here.

Constructing Terminal Ingredients for Linear Systems¶

The conditions of Theorem 1 look abstract, but for a linear system xk+1=Axk+Buk\mathbf x_{k+1}=A\mathbf x_k+B\mathbf u_kxk+1​=Axk​+Buk​ with quadratic stage cost x⊤Qx+u⊤Ru\mathbf x^\top Q\mathbf x+\mathbf u^\top R\mathbf ux⊤Qx+u⊤Ru, they can be met with two matrix computations and one scalar.

Terminal controller and cost. Choose a linear terminal controller πf(x)=Kx\pi_f(\mathbf x)=K\mathbf xπf​(x)=Kx whose closed-loop matrix AK=A+BKA_K=A+BKAK​=A+BK has all eigenvalues inside the unit circle, and a quadratic terminal cost cN(x)=x⊤Pxc_N(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xcN​(x)=x⊤Px. Substituting into the Lyapunov decrease condition gives

x⊤(AK⊤PAK−P+Q+K⊤RK)x≤0for all x∈Xf.\mathbf x^\top\big(A_K^\top PA_K-P+Q+K^\top RK\big)\mathbf x\le0\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X_f .x⊤(AK⊤​PAK​−P+Q+K⊤RK)x≤0for all x∈Xf​.
(21)

The condition holds with equality for every x\mathbf xx when PPP solves the discrete Lyapunov equation

AK⊤PAK−P+Q+K⊤RK=0.A_K^\top PA_K-P+Q+K^\top RK=0 .AK⊤​PAK​−P+Q+K⊤RK=0.
(22)

Because AKA_KAK​ is stable, the solution is unique and equals the series P=∑k=0∞(AK⊤)k(Q+K⊤RK)AKkP=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(A_K^\top)^k(Q+K^\top RK)A_K^kP=∑k=0∞​(AK⊤​)k(Q+K⊤RK)AKk​. Hence x⊤Px\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xx⊤Px is exactly the cost of following u=Kx\mathbf u=K\mathbf xu=Kx forever from x\mathbf xx, provided no constraint is violated along the way. With this choice, the terminal cost is no longer a guess at the tail. It is the cost of one admissible tail.

Any stabilizing KKK works. The natural choice is the gain that makes this tail as cheap as possible, the infinite-horizon linear-quadratic regulator. Its PPP solves the discrete algebraic Riccati equation and its gain is K=−(R+B⊤PB)−1B⊤PAK=-(R+B^\top PB)^{-1}B^\top PAK=−(R+B⊤PB)−1B⊤PA. These formulas are derived by dynamic programming in Finite-Horizon Dynamic Programming. The argument here needs only the Lyapunov equation, which the LQR pair satisfies.

Terminal set. The tail cost is meaningful only where KxK\mathbf xKx respects the constraints for all future steps. Take an ellipsoid Eα={x:x⊤Px≤α}\mathcal E_\alpha=\{\mathbf x:\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha\}Eα​={x:x⊤Px≤α}. It is invariant under AKA_KAK​ for every α\alphaα: by the Lyapunov equation,

(AKx)⊤P(AKx)=x⊤Px−x⊤(Q+K⊤RK)x≤x⊤Px≤α.(A_K\mathbf x)^\top P(A_K\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x-\mathbf x^\top(Q+K^\top RK)\mathbf x\le\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha .(AK​x)⊤P(AK​x)=x⊤Px−x⊤(Q+K⊤RK)x≤x⊤Px≤α.
(23)

It remains to choose α\alphaα so that every constraint holds inside Eα\mathcal E_\alphaEα​. Write each constraint, after substituting u=Kx\mathbf u=K\mathbf xu=Kx, as a pair of half-spaces ±a⊤x≤h\pm\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le h±a⊤x≤h. For the stick, the rows are a=K⊤\mathbf a=K^\topa=K⊤ with h=umax⁡h=u_{\max}h=umax​, and a=(1,0)\mathbf a=(1,0)a=(1,0) with h=θmax⁡h=\theta_{\max}h=θmax​. The largest value of a⊤x\mathbf a^\top\mathbf xa⊤x on Eα\mathcal E_\alphaEα​ is α a⊤P−1a\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}αa⊤P−1a​, a short Lagrange-multiplier computation that the exercises ask for. α=min⁡rows h2a⊤P−1a.\alpha=\min_{\text{rows}}\ \frac{h^2}{\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}.α=rowsmin​ a⊤P−1ah2​.

With Xf=Eα\mathcal X_f=\mathcal E_\alphaXf​=Eα​, both conditions of the theorem hold. Invariance and constraint satisfaction hold by construction, and the decrease holds with equality. This is the construction of Chen & Allgöwer (1998), specialized to linear models. For a nonlinear model, the same recipe is applied to the linearization at the equilibrium, with α\alphaα reduced until the neglected nonlinear terms are dominated.

For the stick, the LQR gain is K=(−23.69, −7.55)K=(-23.69,\,-7.55)K=(−23.69,−7.55), and the input bound is the binding row, giving α=4.02\alpha=4.02α=4.02. Two numerical checks in the build script confirm the construction. Iterating the finite-horizon Riccati recursion from P=QP=QP=Q converges to the same PPP to within 3×10−123\times10^{-12}3×10−12, and on 2000 random points of Xf\mathcal X_fXf​, the largest value of cN(AKx)−cN(x)+c(x,Kx)c_N(A_K\mathbf x)-c_N(\mathbf x)+c(\mathbf x,K\mathbf x)cN​(AK​x)−cN​(x)+c(x,Kx) is of order 10-15, which is zero to rounding.

Suboptimality Bounds¶

How does the finite-horizon value VN(x)V_N(\mathbf x)VN​(x) compare with the infinite-horizon value V∞(x)V_\infty(\mathbf x)V∞​(x) of the constrained problem? The answer depends on the terminal ingredients, and the three choices used on the stick give three different answers. Figure 4 plots them.

Without terminal ingredients, VNV_NVN​ is a lower bound. Take the optimal infinite sequence and keep its first NNN commands. They are feasible for the NNN-step problem, and their cost omits only non-negative tail terms. Hence VN(x)≤V∞(x)V_N(\mathbf x)\le V_\infty(\mathbf x)VN​(x)≤V∞​(x). The same argument shows that VNV_NVN​ is non-decreasing in NNN. On the stick, V1=0.76V_1=0.76V1​=0.76 and V10=13.57V_{10}=13.57V10​=13.57, against V∞=20.15V_\infty=20.15V∞​=20.15.

With a terminal cost alone, VNV_NVN​ is neither. The LQR terminal cost x⊤Px\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xx⊤Px is the cost of the unconstrained tail u=Kx\mathbf u=K\mathbf xu=Kx. Outside Xf\mathcal X_fXf​, that tail violates a constraint, and its cost can be lower than that of any admissible tail. With N=1N=1N=1, the stick gives V1=17.38<V∞V_1=17.38<V_\inftyV1​=17.38<V∞​. An upper bound cannot be obtained without the terminal set.

With terminal cost and terminal set, VNV_NVN​ is an upper bound. Every feasible NNN-step plan, extended by πf\pi_fπf​ from its terminal state, is an admissible infinite sequence. By the Lyapunov equation, its cost equals the NNN-step objective, because cNc_NcN​ is exactly the cost of the extension. The infinite-horizon problem can choose among more sequences, so V∞(x)≤VN(x)V_\infty(\mathbf x)\le V_N(\mathbf x)V∞​(x)≤VN​(x) on XN\mathcal X_NXN​. The bound requires that cNc_NcN​ be at least the cost of following πf\pi_fπf​ from every point of Xf\mathcal X_fXf​. A terminal cost that underestimates that tail loses the upper bound.

Deriving the Approximation Error¶

The interesting question is bounding the approximation error εN=VN(x)−V∞(x)≥0\varepsilon_N=V_N(\mathbf x)-V_\infty(\mathbf x)\ge0εN​=VN​(x)−V∞​(x)≥0 in the third case. It represents the cost of being forced to use πf\pi_fπf​ beyond the horizon rather than continuing to optimize.

Let (u0⋆,u1⋆,…)(\mathbf{u}_0^\star, \mathbf{u}_1^\star, \ldots)(u0⋆​,u1⋆​,…) denote the infinite-horizon optimal control sequence with corresponding state trajectory (x0⋆,x1⋆,…)(\mathbf{x}_0^\star, \mathbf{x}_1^\star, \ldots)(x0⋆​,x1⋆​,…) where x0⋆=x\mathbf{x}_0^\star = \mathbf{x}x0⋆​=x. The infinite-horizon cost is:

V∞(x)=∑k=0∞c(xk⋆,uk⋆)V_\infty(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star)V∞​(x)=k=0∑∞​c(xk⋆​,uk⋆​)
(25)

Suppose the horizon is long enough that this optimal trajectory has entered the terminal set by step NNN, so that xN⋆∈Xf\mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_fxN⋆​∈Xf​. Then its first NNN commands are feasible for the NNN-step problem, with cost

V~N(x)=∑k=0N−1c(xk⋆,uk⋆)+cN(xN⋆)\tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star) + c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star)V~N​(x)=k=0∑N−1​c(xk⋆​,uk⋆​)+cN​(xN⋆​)
(26)

where cN(xN⋆)c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star)cN​(xN⋆​) approximates the tail cost ∑k=N∞c(xk⋆,uk⋆)\sum_{k=N}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star)∑k=N∞​c(xk⋆​,uk⋆​).

Since VN(x)V_N(\mathbf{x})VN​(x) is the optimal NNN-horizon cost (which may do better than this particular truncated sequence), we have VN(x)≤V~N(x)V_N(\mathbf{x}) \leq \tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x})VN​(x)≤V~N​(x). The approximation error therefore satisfies:

εN≤V~N(x)−V∞(x)=cN(xN⋆)−∑k=N∞c(xk⋆,uk⋆)\varepsilon_N \leq \tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x}) - V_\infty(\mathbf{x}) = c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star) - \sum_{k=N}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star)εN​≤V~N​(x)−V∞​(x)=cN​(xN⋆​)−k=N∑∞​c(xk⋆​,uk⋆​)
(27)

This bound shows that the approximation error depends on how well the terminal cost approximates the optimal tail cost along the infinite-horizon optimal trajectory, once that trajectory has entered Xf\mathcal X_fXf​. If xN⋆∉Xf\mathbf x_N^\star\notin\mathcal X_fxN⋆​∈/Xf​, the truncated sequence is infeasible for the NNN-step problem and the bound says nothing.

The stick shows the extreme case. Inside Xf\mathcal X_fXf​, the LQR law satisfies every constraint, so it is optimal for the constrained problem too, and cN=V∞c_N=V_\inftycN​=V∞​ there. The bound then gives εN=0\varepsilon_N=0εN​=0 as soon as xN⋆∈Xf\mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_fxN⋆​∈Xf​, which is what Figure 4 shows from N=9N=9N=9 on. Combined with property 3 of the theorem,

V∞(x0)≤∑tc(xt,κN(xt))≤VN(x0)=V∞(x0),V_\infty(\mathbf x_0)\le\sum_{t}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0)=V_\infty(\mathbf x_0),V∞​(x0​)≤t∑​c(xt​,κN​(xt​))≤VN​(x0​)=V∞​(x0​),
(28)

so the closed-loop cost equals V∞V_\inftyV∞​, as measured. On systems where the optimal tail is not linear, εN\varepsilon_NεN​ is positive and shrinks with NNN at a rate set by how fast optimal trajectories approach Xf\mathcal X_fXf​.

Summary and Outlook¶

Receding-horizon control turns a finite-horizon optimizer into feedback by reinitializing it from each measured state and applying only the first planned action. The result is a state-feedback law κN\kappa_NκN​, defined on the feasible set XN\mathcal X_NXN​ and evaluated by optimization. On the balancing stick, replanning with a wrong model keeps the stick upright, while under the same plan executed open loop the stick falls within a second.

A short horizon alone guarantees nothing. It can leave an unstable system uncontrolled, lose feasibility, or create a spurious equilibrium near a constraint. A terminal cost, a terminal set, and an invariant local controller connect the truncated problem to the infinite-horizon one. The shifted candidate sequence then proves recursive feasibility, a decreasing value, and a closed-loop cost no larger than VN(x0)V_N(\mathbf x_0)VN​(x0​). For linear systems, the terminal cost solves a Lyapunov equation, and the terminal set is an ellipsoid whose size follows from the constraints in closed form.

The basic loop leaves several design choices unresolved. How should the same replanning mechanism represent tracking, economic objectives, uncertainty, hybrid decisions, solver failures, and hard real-time deadlines? MPC variants and reliable operation organize those choices. The guarantees here also assumed an exact model, and the robust and stochastic formulations of that chapter address what replaces them.

Exercises¶

Exercise 1 (A scalar unstable plant)

Consider xk+1=2xk+ukx_{k+1}=2x_k+u_kxk+1​=2xk​+uk​ with ∣uk∣≤1|u_k|\le1∣uk​∣≤1 and stage cost x2+u2x^2+u^2x2+u2.

  1. Show that one-step MPC without terminal ingredients applies u=0u=0u=0 from every state, and conclude that it does not stabilize the origin.

Exercise 2 (One step with the LQR terminal cost)

Let PPP solve the discrete algebraic Riccati equation for (A,B,Q,R)(A,B,Q,R)(A,B,Q,R), and let K=−(R+B⊤PB)−1B⊤PAK=-(R+B^\top PB)^{-1}B^\top PAK=−(R+B⊤PB)−1B⊤PA. Show that one-step MPC with terminal cost x⊤Px\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xx⊤Px and no active constraints applies exactly u=Kx\mathbf u=K\mathbf xu=Kx. Which curve of Figure 4 does this explain at N=1N=1N=1, and why does that value lie below V∞V_\inftyV∞​?

Solution to Exercise 2

The objective is x⊤Qx+u⊤Ru+(Ax+Bu)⊤P(Ax+Bu)\mathbf x^\top Q\mathbf x+\mathbf u^\top R\mathbf u+(A\mathbf x+B\mathbf u)^\top P(A\mathbf x+B\mathbf u)x⊤Qx+u⊤Ru+(Ax+Bu)⊤P(Ax+Bu). Setting its gradient in u\mathbf uu to zero gives (R+B⊤PB)u=−B⊤PAx(R+B^\top PB)\mathbf u=-B^\top PA\mathbf x(R+B⊤PB)u=−B⊤PAx, which is u=Kx\mathbf u=K\mathbf xu=Kx. Without constraints, its value is x⊤Px\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf xx⊤Px by the Riccati equation, the unconstrained infinite-horizon cost. This is the green curve at N=1N=1N=1. From x0=(0.2,0.6)\mathbf x_0=(0.2,0.6)x0​=(0.2,0.6), the unconstrained LQR tail exceeds the command bound, so it is cheaper than every admissible tail, and the value 17.38 lies below the constrained V∞=20.15V_\infty=20.15V∞​=20.15.

Exercise 3 (Support function of an ellipsoid)

Let PPP be symmetric positive definite and α>0\alpha>0α>0. Show that max⁡{a⊤x:x⊤Px≤α}=α a⊤P−1a\max\{\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x:\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha\}=\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}max{a⊤x:x⊤Px≤α}=αa⊤P−1a​, and deduce the formula for the terminal level α\alphaα.

Solution to Exercise 3

The maximum of a linear function over the ellipsoid is attained on its boundary. Stationarity of a⊤x−λ(x⊤Px−α)\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x-\lambda(\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x-\alpha)a⊤x−λ(x⊤Px−α) gives x=P−1a/(2λ)\mathbf x=P^{-1}\mathbf a/(2\lambda)x=P−1a/(2λ). Substituting into x⊤Px=α\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x=\alphax⊤Px=α gives 2λ=a⊤P−1a/α2\lambda=\sqrt{\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a/\alpha}2λ=a⊤P−1a/α​, and the value is a⊤P−1a/(2λ)=α a⊤P−1a\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a/(2\lambda)=\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}a⊤P−1a/(2λ)=αa⊤P−1a​. The half-space a⊤x≤h\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le ha⊤x≤h contains the ellipsoid exactly when this value is at most hhh, that is, when α≤h2/(a⊤P−1a)\alpha\le h^2/(\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a)α≤h2/(a⊤P−1a). By symmetry, the same condition covers −a⊤x≤h-\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le h−a⊤x≤h. Taking the minimum over all rows gives α\alphaα.

Exercise 4 (The spurious equilibrium)

Using code/receding_horizon.py, run the controller without terminal ingredients with N=5N=5N=5 from (0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.6) for 200 steps. Inspect the final state, the applied command, and the predicted trajectory of the last subproblem. Explain why the state is a fixed point of the closed loop, and why it is not a fixed point of the open-loop dynamics with u=0u=0u=0. Find the smallest horizon for which the stick returns upright from this initial state.

Solution to Exercise 4

The closed loop settles at θ˙=0\dot\theta=0θ˙=0, θ≈0.32\theta\approx0.32θ≈0.32 rad, with a constant command close to −(g/ℓ) θ≈−3.1-(g/\ell)\,\theta\approx-3.1−(g/ℓ)θ≈−3.1 rad/s2^22, which cancels the gravitational acceleration. The last plan holds the stick nearly still, and its predicted angle approaches the limit at the end of the horizon. Within five steps, pushing the stick back costs more command effort than it saves in angle cost, so the plan that holds the state is optimal, and applying its first command reproduces the same state. With u=0u=0u=0, the same state falls away. With N=6N=6N=6, the stick still parks, near θ≈0.29\theta\approx0.29θ≈0.29 rad. N=7N=7N=7 is the smallest horizon that returns it upright within 200 steps, with closed-loop cost 34.1, and N=8N=8N=8 lowers that cost to 24.1.

Exercise 5 (Where the proof breaks under model error)

Repeat the replanning experiment of Figure 1, and record VN(xt)V_N(\mathbf x_t)VN​(xt​) along the closed loop. Identify each step where VN(xt+1)>VN(xt)−c(xt,ut)V_N(\mathbf x_{t+1})>V_N(\mathbf x_t)-c(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf u_t)VN​(xt+1​)>VN​(xt​)−c(xt​,ut​). Which line of the proof of Theorem 1 fails at those steps? Then shorten the plant’s stick further and find the length at which the replanned controller first meets an infeasible subproblem.

Solution to Exercise 5

The proof assumes x+=x1⋆\mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\starx+=x1⋆​. The tap violates that assumption by 0.5 rad/s in one step, and VNV_NVN​ jumps from 0.61 to 3.23. The shorter stick violates it by a small amount at every step, so the decrease inequality can fail by a margin even where VNV_NVN​ keeps decreasing. The shifted candidate is built from the predicted state, so it need not be feasible from the measured one. Recursive feasibility is no longer guaranteed, and for a short enough stick it fails. The threshold depends on the tap and the initial state, which is why robust MPC tightens the constraints by bounds on the prediction error.

Exercise 6 (A rate limit in the terminal set)

Add the constraint ∣θ˙k∣≤1|\dot\theta_k|\le1∣θ˙k​∣≤1 rad/s to the stick through StickParameters(rate_max=1.0). Recompute α\alphaα and state which row is now binding. Recompute the feasible sets of Figure 2 and check whether κ20\kappa_{20}κ20​ still agrees with sat⁡(Kx)\operatorname{sat}(K\mathbf x)sat(Kx).

Solution to Exercise 6

The terminal level becomes the minimum over three rows. For the rate row, a=(0,1)\mathbf a=(0,1)a=(0,1) and h=1h=1h=1 give h2/(a⊤P−1a)≈4.39h^2/(\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a)\approx4.39h2/(a⊤P−1a)≈4.39. For the angle row the value is 8.99, and for the input row 4.02. The input bound still binds, so α\alphaα and Xf\mathcal X_fXf​ do not change, although the rate bound comes close. The function terminal_level performs the same computation. The feasible sets are cut by the horizontal lines θ˙=±1\dot\theta=\pm1θ˙=±1. Where the rate bound becomes active along the optimal predicted path, the first command can differ from the saturated linear law, so measure the gap rather than assume it.

Computational Sources¶

The model, the MPC subproblem, and the checks are in one module, and the figures and numbers are produced by one script:

  • Balancing-stick model and linear MPC

  • Experiment and figure builder

  • Numbers quoted in this chapter

Run uv run python scripts/build_receding_horizon_artifacts.py from the repository root to regenerate the four figures and the metrics, in about one minute. Normal book builds read the saved figures. The tests in tests/test_receding_horizon.py check the Lyapunov equation, the terminal level, the shifted-candidate inequality, recursive feasibility, and the bounds on VNV_NVN​ on short runs.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 7 (Receding horizon)

An MPC solver returns a sequence (u0⋆,…,uN−1⋆)(\mathbf{u}_0^\star,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{N-1}^\star)(u0⋆​,…,uN−1⋆​). Which controls are normally applied before the problem is solved again?

Solution to Exercise 7

Only the first control (or first short control block) is applied. The state is measured again and the horizon is shifted before re-optimizing.

Exercise 8 (Terminal ingredients)

What roles do a terminal cost and a terminal constraint play in finite-horizon MPC?

Solution to Exercise 8

The terminal cost approximates value beyond the horizon; the terminal constraint can keep the endpoint in a region from which a known controller remains feasible and stable.

Exercise 9 (Disturbance response)

Why does resolving the same finite-horizon optimization after each measurement provide feedback even if the prediction model is deterministic?

Solution to Exercise 9

The newly measured state contains the accumulated effect of disturbances and model error. Reinitializing the optimization from that state changes the planned controls accordingly.
